draft.title: Neutralisation reactions
card: In a neutralisation reaction, an acid reacts with a base to form a salt and water. The salt is an ionic compound made from the positive ion of the base and the negative ion of the acid.
Example: HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H2O(l). Here the salt is sodium chloride.
Neutralisation releases heat, so it is exothermic. The enthalpy of neutralisation is the heat released when an acid and a base react to form one mole of water.
A neutralisation reaction does not always give a solution with pH 7. The final pH depends on the acid and base used, and on whether one of them is left over.
draft.remember: Acid + base → salt + water, and heat is released.

a.q: Which pair of products forms when sulfuric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide?
a.why: An acid and a base form a salt and water. The salt is made of the sodium ion from the base and the sulfate ion from the acid. Hydrogen gas is not a product here, because that pattern belongs to a different type of reaction.
a.clue: Name the salt, then add the other product.

b.q: Tahlia mixes dilute hydrochloric acid with dilute potassium hydroxide in a beaker. The beaker feels warm. What explains this?
opts: Neutralisation is exothermic, so it releases heat
Neutralisation is endothermic, so it absorbs heat
The salt that forms dissolves and heats the water
The acid and base are both warm before mixing
b.why: Neutralisation releases heat to the surroundings, so the mixture warms up. This heat is the enthalpy of neutralisation. An endothermic reaction would make the beaker feel cool, not warm.
b.clue: Think about which way heat moves when the beaker feels warm.

b.best: Neutralisation is exothermic, so it releases heat
